newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia's U.S. friends, former foe applaud Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Asia's U.S. friends, former foe applaud Clinton.

text.p: Asian allies, sparring partners and a former foe of the United States joined in congratulating Bill Clinton on his re-election on Wednesday, with most major countries saying his win could only help regional stability.
China, which has been at odds with the United States on issues ranging from trade to Taiwan, congratulated Clinton and said it was ready to work with the United States for further progress.

"We wish to congratulate President Clinton on his re-election... Now, a good opportunity has presented itself for improving and expanding Sino-U.S. relations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai told reporters.
Japan, preoccupied with putting its own house in order, savoured Clinton's re-election as a sign there were no dramatic U-turns ahead in relations with its main ally.
Sometimes awkward ties between the two countries have improved this year after progress over trade issues and the U.S. military presence on Okinawa.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who goes through the formality of being re-elected prime minister by parliament on Thursday, was unstinting in his praise, saying he congratulated the president "from the bottom of my heart".
"The people of the United States made a very great choice," he told reporters.
Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said: "President Clinton's re-election reassures us of world peace and prosperity."
Clinton will meet Chinese and Japanese leaders, as well as other regional heads of government or state, in the Philippines later this month at the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting.
Former U.S. foe Vietnam joined the applause for Clinton, who normalised relations between Washington and Hanoi last year two decades after the communists won the Vietnam War.

"On our side, Vietnam hopes the cooperative relationship between Vietnam and the United States will continue to develop for the benefit of the two countries and the benefit of peace, stability, cooperation and development in the region and world," a foreign ministry spokesman said, reading from a statement.
South Korea, a longtime U.S. ally, welcomed the result. President Kim Young-sam sent a telegram to Clinton expressing hopes for better bilateral ties, Kim's spokeman said.
"I hope our joint efforts to achieve stability and peace on the Korean peninsula will bear fruit in the near future," he said.

Clinton and Kim earlier this year jointly proposed four- nation peace talks involving their nations and North Korea and China aimed at replacing with a peace treaty the truce agreement that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
There was no immediate word from North Korea or Burma, both Asian states which have long jousted with U.S. governments.
Only India, unsure how Clinton would react to New Delhi's global nuclear standoff during a second term in office, appeared lukewarm.
"We'll have to take a positive view. India never took sides in any U.S. election," a foreign ministry official said. "So we'll hope for the best."

Southeast Asian countries offered garlands. Indonesian president Suharto and his Philippine counterpart Fidel Ramos sent congratulations, while Thailand expressed the hope Clinton would continue to strengthen his country's presence in Asia.

"Certainly we want to see closer relations. Especially we would like to see the United States come to play a key role in this region, we do not want them to pull back," Thai Foreign Minister Amnuay Viravan said.
Further south, Australian Prime Minister John Howard said he was looking forward to welcoming Clinton and his wife Hillary to Australia later this month.
"Your leadership and that of the nation you have been re-elected to lead are both critical to the peace and stability of the world," Howard wrote in a letter to Clinton.
